entries.title: Reading the First Term Mathematics figures: binary ladders, tally table and charts
entries.body:
Objectives: read the recovered division ladders, tally table, pictogram and charts correctly; spot and correct printed slips by calculation.
Newly prepared teaching: this lesson explains the figures attached to the First Term notes on Binary numbers and Everyday statistics. It does not replace the school notes.
Binary ladders. Divide by 2 repeatedly, write each remainder beside its quotient, stop at quotient 0, and read the remainders from the bottom upwards. Ladder for 8: 8 / 2 = 4 R 0; 4 / 2 = 2 R 0; 2 / 2 = 1 R 0; 1 / 2 = 0 R 1; reading upwards gives 1000 in base two. The printed ladder (a) leaves out the row 2 / 2 = 1 R 0 and so shows only three remainders; the complete ladder has four. Ladder for 107: 53 R 1, 26 R 1, 13 R 0, 6 R 1, 3 R 0, 1 R 1, 0 R 1; reading upwards gives 1101011 in base two. Check: 64 + 32 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 107. The printed result 11010011 equals 211, so it is a slip; the ladder itself is right.
Mixed number. 10.1001 in base two = 2 + 1/2 + 1/16 = 2 9/16 (= 41/16) in base ten; the note's flattened text 29/16 is the mixed number 2 9/16, not the fraction 29/16 (which would be 1.8125).
Binary arithmetic labels. The worked examples are Add 101111 and 10011, then Subtract; the columns are printed the other way round. Check: 47 + 19 = 66 = 1000010 in base two, and 47 - 19 = 28 = 11100. Multiplication 1101 x 111: partial products 1101, 11010, 110100 add to 1011011 (13 x 7 = 91). Division: 10010001 / 101 = 11101 (145 / 5 = 29). The printed long-division bracket shows 1001001 (73), which is not divisible by 101, so it cannot give 11101; use the figures here: the first four digits 1001 contain 101 once with remainder 100, and bringing down the remaining digits one at a time ends with remainder 0.
Tally and frequency table. The 30 phone-call values give frequencies 3, 7, 4, 9, 5, 0, 2 for 4 to 10 calls (total 30). The printed tally for 5 calls shows six strokes; it should show seven (one crossed group of five and two more). Pictogram: one large car = 2, one small car = 1; black 10 large, white 8 large + 1 small, red 4, yellow 2 + 1 small, green 5.
Charts. The dual bar chart in the notes was plotted with girls 45, 55, 75, 90, 65, but the table in the same note gives 46, 55, 73, 92, 64; the two differ in 1997, 1999, 2000 and 2001, while the boys' figures (65, 50, 80, 70, 45) agree. The notes do not say which set was meant. Source decision (21 October 2026, owner-directed interim decision by the app owner; not yet confirmed by the school's Mathematics teacher): the table is correct, so the solution here is drawn from the table values. The chart in the notes is shown as printed and is not edited; where its bars differ, read the table value. Solution to the note's questions, from the table: the year girls had the highest admission is 2000 (92); the year boys had the least admission is 2001 (45); in 1999 boys had 80 - 73 = 7 more admissions than girls; in 2000 there were (70 + 92) - (50 + 55) = 162 - 105 = 57 more candidates than in 1998. Reading the printed chart instead would give 5 and 55 for the last two; those are not used. In the pie chart example, the share for building projects is 70 / 150 x 100 = 46.7 per cent (not degrees); the sector angle is 168 degrees.
Practice questions (newly prepared equivalents, not from the school notes or a textbook page): 1. Convert 45 and 100 to base two with a ladder. 2. Add 1101 and 101 in base two. 3. Using the table values, in which year did girls have the highest admission, and what is the difference between boys and girls in 1999? 4. A pie chart shows 25 of 150 as one sector; find its angle and percentage.
Answers and marking guide: 1. 45 = 101101 and 100 = 1100100 (check by place value). 2. 1101 + 101 = 10010 (13 + 5 = 18). 3. 2000 (92); 1999 difference 80 - 73 = 7. 4. 25 / 150 x 360 = 60 degrees and 25 / 150 x 100 = 16.7 per cent. Award a mark for the method and a mark for the check by converting back to base ten.

entries.title: Reading the Second Term Mathematics figures: triangles, elevation, depression and bearings
entries.body:
Objectives: name the sides of a right triangle from a marked angle; use the trigonometric ratios on the recovered figures; read elevation, depression and bearing diagrams correctly.
Newly prepared teaching: this lesson explains the figures attached to the Second Term notes on the trigonometric ratios, their applications and bearings. It does not replace the school notes.
Naming sides. In the recovered triangle ABC the right angle is at A. Relative to angle B, side AB is adjacent, side AC is opposite and BC is the hypotenuse, so sin B = AC / BC, cos B = AB / BC and tan B = AC / AB.
Exercise triangles (newly prepared answer key; the marked-angle symbol in the file is U+2205 and its intended name is not decided, so it is called "the marked angle"). (a) The vertical side 5 cm is opposite the marked angle at C and the hypotenuse is 12 cm: sin C = 5 / 12, so C = 24.6 degrees. (b) Side BC = 14 cm lies next to the marked angle at C and the hypotenuse is 30 cm: cos C = 14 / 30, so C = 62.2 degrees.
Worked figures already in the notes, checked: ladder x = 10 sin 30 = 5 m; tower tan(angle) = 50 / 80 = 0.625, angle = 32.0 degrees; cliff x = 150 / tan 20 = 412 m (the angle of depression at A equals the angle of elevation 20 degrees at C because they are alternate angles).
Assignment triangle PQR. The foot of the 140 cm line is not labelled in the figure although the question mentions S. Assumption, stated plainly (21 October 2026, owner-directed interim decision by the app owner; not yet confirmed by the school's Mathematics teacher): S is the foot of the perpendicular from Q, where the right-angle mark is. This is the only reading that fits the figure, because the 140 cm line cannot be the slant side QR when SR is 200 cm. Then tan(angle QRS) = 140 / 200, so angle QRS = 35.0 degrees; PS = 140 tan 30 = 80.8 cm and PR = 80.8 + 200 = 280.8 cm. Check by another route: QR = square root of (140 squared + 200 squared) = 244.1 cm, angle SQR = 90 - 35.0 = 55.0 degrees, angle PQR = 30 + 55.0 = 85.0 degrees, angle P = 90 - 30 = 60 degrees, and the sine rule gives PR = 244.1 x sin 85.0 / sin 60 = 280.8 cm. A different position for S would give different answers.
Bearings. A bearing is measured clockwise from north in three figures. The compass figure shows N 000, NE 045, E 090, SE 135, S 180, SW 225, W 270, NW 315. In bearing example 1 the vertical arrow runs due north from the corner (call the corner O) to A and the horizontal arrow runs due east from O to B. Source decision (21 October 2026, owner-directed interim decision by the app owner; not yet confirmed by the school's Mathematics teacher): follow the drawing. So the bearing of B from O is 090 degrees and the bearing of A from O is 000 degrees. The note's sentence "The bearing of point A from B is 090" does not match the drawing and is not used. Back bearings follow from the drawing by adding or subtracting 180 degrees: O from B is 270 degrees and O from A is 180 degrees. The bearing of A from B cannot be given as one number without the distances OA and OB: it lies between 270 and 360 degrees (north-west of B) and is exactly 315 degrees only when OA = OB. In example 2 the arrow to P is drawn at 225 degrees although the label says 210 degrees; the drawing is not to scale, so use the label 210 degrees.
Practice questions (newly prepared equivalents, not from the school notes or a textbook page): 1. A ladder 8 m long makes 60 degrees with the ground; how high up the wall does it reach? 2. From a point 40 m from a tree the angle of elevation of the top is 30 degrees; find the height. 3. P is 30 km north and Q is 20 km west of R; find the bearing of Q from P. 4. A boat is 50 m from the base of a 20 m cliff; find the angle of depression. 5. In bearing example 1, state the bearing of B from O, of A from O, of O from B and of O from A.
Answers and marking guide: 1. 8 sin 60 = 6.93 m. 2. 40 tan 30 = 23.1 m. 3. Q from P is 20 km west and 30 km south, so the bearing is 180 + arctan(20/30) = 213.7 degrees. 4. tan = 20 / 50 = 0.4, angle = 21.8 degrees. 5. 090, 000, 270 and 180 degrees (a back bearing is the bearing plus or minus 180). Award a mark for a labelled sketch, a mark for choosing the right ratio and a mark for the answer.
